rubrics.criterion: Maintenance-plan selection for the indexing engine is owned by the index component again: which node to checkpoint, compact, garbage-collect, expire or take into backup, and the backup-completion transition, are decided by index-side code reading index node and queue state, and the scheduler contains no multi-branch selection cascade that evaluates those matching conditions itself.
rubrics.rationale: Plan selection is the first responsibility the scheduler absorbed in this case; the whole six-way matching cascade (LSN bounds, cache-per-node watermark, duplicated-key ratio, expiry timestamps, backup bounds, delayed node-gc list) had its previous owner deleted, so ownership restoration is the core of the task.

rubrics.criterion: Per-database statistics aggregation is owned by the index component again: node counts, stored and in-memory key counts, duplicate counts, index sizes, page counts, memory used and disk/cache read counters are computed by index-side code, and no scheduler procedure walks the index node tree to derive those totals.
rubrics.rationale: The index component's statistics module and its record type were deleted outright in this case, so a complete repair must re-establish engine-side aggregation rather than merely re-pointing callers at some other existing walker.

rubrics.criterion: Write-ahead-log maintenance policy is owned by the log component again: the rotation-readiness decision against the configured watermark and the sweep of completed garbage files live behind the log component's interface, and the scheduler step loop no longer inspects the log manager's file list, completion state or unlock/sweep conditions directly.
rubrics.rationale: The scheduler in this case took over both the rotation-readiness rule and the garbage sweep while the log component kept only the physical rotate/gc acts; un-splitting that policy requires restoring log-side decisions without breaking the externally driven log commands.

rubrics.criterion: Every scheduler dispatch center that requests a maintenance plan - the background task loop's queue-driven operations, the directly driven checkpoint/compaction/node-gc sites, and the manual compaction control command - obtains plans through the re-owned engine interface, while per-queue worker admission limits are still applied by the scheduler before a plan is accepted.
rubrics.rationale: This case had two distinct caller classes of the absorbed cascade (background loop and operator command) plus a purpose-kept admission gate; a repair that rewires only the obvious loop sites would leave the control command on a stale path or drop the admission discipline.

rubrics.criterion: The runtime status and configuration serialization path obtains each database's snapshot through the owning components' own interfaces - scheduler state from the scheduler and index statistics from the index - without any scheduler procedure producing a merged engine-and-scheduling statistics snapshot.
rubrics.rationale: The environment's per-database status block was rewired in this case to a single merged, scheduler-produced snapshot and its record member layout changed with it; the reporting path is the only consumer that must be re-connected once the responsibility moves home.

rubrics.criterion: The maintenance worker trace still renders every selected plan with the same strings, node identifiers and step ordering as before the refactor (checkpoint, compaction, gc, node gc, expire and backup, including log rotation and log gc markers).
rubrics.rationale: Plan-trace rendering and the two log housekeeping trace markers moved together with the absorbed logic in this case; trace output is directly observable behavior of the worker loop that the refactor must carry across components unchanged.

rubrics.criterion: The scheduler does not retain dead or duplicated copies of the absorbed logic after the ownership moves: no unused scheduler-side procedures, prototypes or headers for the plan-selection cascade, the statistics walk, or the log maintenance policy remain behind, and the scheduler build list matches the scheduler's surviving sources.
rubrics.rationale: A partial repair in this case would typically relocate the engine-side interfaces and leave the old scheduler-side modules and their declarations as unreachable residue; leftover scheduler-owned copies of engine policy are the direct residue of the injected design.

rubrics.criterion: No dangling references to moved or removed maintenance code exist anywhere in the tree: every declared maintenance interface has a definition in the component that owns it, every component build list and include list matches the files that exist, and no consumer calls a scheduler-owned variant of an engine responsibility that was relocated back.
rubrics.rationale: This case touched declaration surfaces, component headers and both component builds across four modules; cleanup of those wirings is instance-specific (two makefile lists, two component headers, several prototype surfaces), not generic hygiene.

rubrics.criterion: The scheduler's per-database summary record no longer lays out another engine's internals: the statistics fields that describe index state are not carried by the scheduler-side record, and each component's record types describe their own component's state.
rubrics.rationale: The scheduler's summary record was redefined in this case as the only place the deleted engine statistics layout had a name; unless that record is re-scoped, the cross-component layout duplication survives even after code moves home.

rubrics.criterion: Plan-selection outcomes are unchanged: under identical index state the same node is selected for each operation, locked nodes are retried rather than selected or dropped, saturated worker queues still yield retry instead of dispatching, compaction selection respects the cache-per-node watermark as before, and backup still transitions to completion only under the original bounds.
rubrics.rationale: The matching semantics in this case are subtle (retry vs skip vs early-exit per operation type, a computed watermark, a fallback transition); a repair that re-implements the cascade from scratch can silently change any of them while still passing a subset of tests.

rubrics.criterion: Log maintenance behavior is unchanged: rotation still occurs exactly when the active file satisfies the rotation watermark and never when the log is disabled, and the garbage sweep removes no file the previous logic would keep (in particular files still being written or referenced for backup).
rubrics.rationale: In this case the readiness rule and the sweep policy were re-implemented inside the scheduler with the act left in the log component; the split makes it easy to duplicate, drop or reorder the enable/disable checks and completion-state tests without any compilation symptom.

rubrics.criterion: The refactored locking discipline is sound in every touched path: the index engine's lock is not acquired while the scheduler mutex is held or vice versa at any point of the restored snapshot and planning paths, no return path leaves a component lock held, and plan requests still take no engine lock out of turn.
rubrics.rationale: The absorbed logic in this case sequences three different synchronization domains (scheduler mutex, index lock, log manager spinlock) that previously never met inside one procedure; an ownership repair that re-splits these paths can create statically-invisible deadlocks or leaked locks only visible under a specific maintenance interleaving.

rubrics.criterion: Reported runtime statistics values are identical to before for the same underlying database state: the scheduler live state and the index aggregates are each sourced from their own component, and neither summary is zeroed, stale, double-counted or cross-assigned after the split.
rubrics.rationale: This case originally merged two separately-locked snapshots into one procedure; splitting it back is exactly where half-initialized or cross-wired record fields would pass compilation and ordinary smoke checks while producing wrong status output.
